title: 0.3 pandas
text: NumPy arrays are fast but anonymous — columns have no names, rows have no identity, and mixed types are impossible. pandas adds labels. It is the Python twin of R’s data frame (the tidyverse’s tibble), and it will be your main tool for loading, cleaning, and summarizing data before any model sees it.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
1. Basic Concept
A DataFrame is a rectangular table: each column is a Series (a labeled 1-D array with one dtype), and rows share an index. Think: dict of columns + shared row labels.






Two selectors, two jobs. loc selects by label, iloc by integer position, and both use [rows, columns]:






groupby is the split–apply–combine engine and probably the single most used pandas verb:






merging joins two tables on a key — the same mental model as SQL joins:

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
2. Concept Questions

What is the difference between df["expr"] and df[["expr"]]?
When do loc and iloc give different answers for the same-looking call?
Why does df[df["expr"] > 10]["expr"] = 0 silently fail to change df?
What does how="left" in merge guarantee, and what can it create?
What does df.groupby("tissue")["expr"].transform("mean") return, and how is it different from .mean()?



Answers


df["expr"] returns a Series; df[["expr"]] returns a one-column DataFrame. Many methods (.T, joining, multiple columns) behave differently on the two.
When the index labels are not 0..n-1 (e.g. after filtering, or a named index). loc["S2", ...] finds the row named S2; iloc[1, ...] finds the second row whatever it’s called.
Chained indexing: the first bracket may return a temporary copy, so the assignment can land on a copy that’s then discarded (the classic SettingWithCopyWarning). The correct form assigns through one loc call: df.loc[df["expr"] > 10, "expr"] = 0.
Left merge keeps every row of the left table; rows with no match on the right get NaN in the right columns (a merge “fan-out” can also multiply rows if the key is duplicated on the right).
transform("mean") returns a Series the same length/index as df — the group mean broadcast back to each row — so you can subtract it to center within groups. .mean() returns one row per group.

text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
We’ll build one small cohort table and predict outputs before running each cell.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. From the cohort df above: build a summary table with one row per group showing mean age, mean marker, and patient count, then add a column is_old (age > 50) and recompute the table splitting on both group and is_old.


Solution







The agg(col=("source", "func")) named aggregation syntax produces clean column names in one pass — no renaming afterwards.

Exercise 2. Merge a measurements table with a demographic table (left join), count missing matches, and fill missing site values with "unknown".


Solution







P03 exists in measurements but not demographics → left join keeps it, site becomes NaN. This exact pattern (merge → count NaN → decide policy) is 90% of real data integration.

Exercise 3. Given the wide expression table below (rows = genes, columns = samples), compute each gene’s mean and variance, keep genes with variance above 2.0, and melt the survivors into long format (gene, sample, value).


Solution







Wide ↔︎ long reshaping (melt / pivot) is the pandas equivalent of tidyverse’s pivot_longer / pivot_wider. Most plotting and modeling tools want long format.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Chained assignment is the #1 pandas bug. df[df.a > 0]["b"] = 1 may write to a temporary copy. Always: single loc call → df.loc[mask, "b"] = 1. (pandas 3.0’s copy-on-write makes chained assignment fail loudly; the pyodide pandas here is 2.x, where it can still silently no-op.)
inplace=True is deprecated style. It mutates the object you may not own and prevents method chaining. Prefer df = df.dropna() or df.dropna(subset=["marker"], inplace=False).
Index is not “row number”. After filtering, .iloc[0] and .index[0] diverge. Reset with reset_index(drop=True) when position and label must agree again.
merge can silently multiply rows if the key is duplicated on either side — always check len(result) vs len(left) and result["key"].value_counts().
== on a column with NaN gives False, never NaN: df[df["x"] == np.nan] matches nothing. Use df["x"].isna().
Object dtype columns are slow (Python objects, not arrays). Convert strings to category when few distinct values; parse dates with pd.to_datetime immediately.
groupby drops groups containing NaN keys by default (dropna=True) — a silent row-loss channel in reports.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run it, observe, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Chained assignment: high may be a copy, so the mark never lands in df (see the printed 0). Fix with df.loc[df["value"] > 10, "site"] = "HIGH".
NaN never equals NaN: count is 0 despite two NaNs. Fix: df["value"].isna().sum().
Loop + manual dict is slower, noisier, and easier to get wrong than groupby; also the loop’s .mean() results are fine here but the pattern invites index bugs. Fix: df.groupby("site")["value"].mean().

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. A colleague merges a 20,000-row measurements table with a 200-row annotation table and the result has 23,117 rows. Diagnose the likely causes and give a defensive merge recipe.


Hint

What does validate= in merge do? What does a duplicated key do to row counts?



Solution

The key is duplicated: an m-to-many join multiplies rows (each left row matches every right row with the same key). Diagnosis: anno["gene"].value_counts().head(), compare len(left), len(right), len(merged); check merged["gene"].is_unique. Defensive recipe: merged = meas.merge(anno, on="gene", how="left", validate="m:1") — raises instead of fanning out; or deduplicate anno.drop_duplicates("gene") first; assert len(merged) == len(meas) afterwards. Choosing validate is documentation and a runtime guard.

Q2. Explain the difference between apply, transform, and agg on a groupby object, and why apply is the dangerous one. Give a task where apply is genuinely required.


Solution

agg collapses each group to one value (len = n groups). transform returns one value per input row (len = n rows, group statistic broadcast back). apply returns whatever your function returns — a scalar, a Series, or a DataFrame — so pandas has to guess how to assemble results, which is slower and produces surprising shapes/indexes. Use agg/transform whenever possible; reach for apply when you need genuinely per-group multi-row computation, e.g. fitting a per-group linear model and returning its coefficients as a Series: df.groupby("site").apply(lambda g: pd.Series(np.polyfit(g["x"], g["y"], 1), index=["slope", "intercept"])). In modern pandas, prefer groupby(...).filter(...) for row selection and named agg for summaries to keep types predictable.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (pandas × 0.4 Visualisation). Take the cohort df and produce, in long format, everything needed to plot marker distributions per group: which table shape does matplotlib’s ax.boxplot want (list of arrays) and which does a pandas .boxplot(by=...) want? Convert between wide and long to produce the same figure both ways — internalize why “tidy/long” is the interchange format and “wide” is a display choice.
C2 (pandas × 1.2 Relationships). For the cohort data, compute the correlation matrix of the numeric columns (df.corr(numeric_only=True)), then compute it within groups (df.groupby("group").corr(numeric_only=True)). Under what real-world condition can the pooled correlation have the opposite sign from every within-group correlation (Simpson’s paradox)? Construct a 3-line synthetic example demonstrating it.

title: 0.3 pandas
text:
7. Summary

A DataFrame is labeled columns of Series sharing an index; dtypes tells you what you actually have.
loc = labels, iloc = positions; filtering is df.loc[mask, cols] — one call, no chaining.
groupby + agg/transform covers split–apply–combine; transform broadcasts back to row shape.
merge(how="left", validate="m:1") with NaN-counting afterwards is the safe join recipe.
NaN: use .isna(), skipna defaults, and decide drop-vs-fill deliberately.
Wide is for humans, long is for machines; melt/pivot convert between them.
Numbers on a page lie less than pictures — next page turns these tables into plots that reveal structure before you model it: 0.4 Visualisation & EDA.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text: Python is the substrate everything else in this course is written in. Before touching NumPy, pandas, or scikit-learn, your reflexes in core Python — types, functions, comprehensions, error messages — need to be automatic. This page drills exactly those reflexes, with a bias toward the numerical/data style of Python rather than web or scripting styles.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
1. Basic Concept
Python is a dynamically typed language: names are labels attached to objects, not boxes with fixed types. For numerical work you mostly live with four scalar types (int, float, bool, str) and four container types (list, tuple, dict, set).
One fact causes more numerical bugs than anything else: Python float is IEEE-754 binary floating point, so most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly.






The second fact to internalize: / is always true division; // is floor division; % is the remainder.






A function is defined with def, returns with return (no return means it returns None), and can take default arguments:






Comprehensions are the idiomatic way to transform collections. If you are writing a for loop whose only job is to build a list, you should usually write a comprehension instead:






f-strings format values into text — you will use them constantly to report results:

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
2. Concept Questions
Answer from memory first, then open each answer to check.

What does 10 / 4 evaluate to, and what type is the result?
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 False? Name the underlying cause.
What is the difference between a list and a tuple? Give one practical consequence.
What does a function return if you never write return?
In f"{x:.2f}", what does the .2f part do?



Answers


2.5, a float. In Python 3, / always produces a float, even for whole-number results (8 / 2 is 4.0).
0.1 and 0.2 have no exact representation in binary floating point (IEEE-754). Their nearest representable values don’t sum to the nearest representable 0.3. Compare with a tolerance (math.isclose) instead.
Lists are mutable, tuples are immutable. Consequence: tuples can be dictionary keys and elements of sets; lists cannot. Also, accidentally mutating a tuple raises an error, which can protect data.
None.
Format x as a fixed-point number with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point (rounding half-to-even on the decimal representation).

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict each line’s output before running. These rebuild reflexes — do them until automatic.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write a function celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) that converts a temperature and returns the result rounded to 1 decimal place. Then use it in a comprehension to convert [0, 37, 100].


Solution








Exercise 2. Given the DNA string below, compute (a) its length, (b) GC content as a percentage with 1 decimal, (c) its reverse complement. Use one comprehension and one dictionary somewhere.


Solution







Note: reversed(seq) + join is O(n); building a string with += in a loop is O(n²) — a classic performance trap.

Exercise 3. FizzBuzz, data edition: for integers 1–20, print Bio if divisible by 3, Stats if divisible by 5, BioStats if divisible by both, otherwise the number — as a single list of strings.


Solution







Order matters: check the compound condition (% 15 == 0) first, otherwise the simple cases win. Same idea as writing mutually exclusive if/elif branches.

Exercise 4. Parse this mini-FASTA (a real task shape in bioinformatics) and report each sequence’s length and GC%:
>gene1
ATGGCC
>gene2
GCGCGCGCGT


Solution







sum(b in "GC" for b in seq) works because True/False sum as 1/0 — an idiom worth owning.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls
Pitfalls that bite numerical/data Python specifically:

Mutable default arguments are created once, at function definition — not at each call. def f(x, acc=[]) shares the same list across all calls. This is the single most common “haunted function” bug.
is compares identity, == compares value. Never write x is 5 — it happens to work for small ints in CPython and breaks everywhere else.
Floats in loops accumulate error. Summing 10 million floats with + loses precision; use math.fsum or better, NumPy (np.sum uses pairwise summation).
Chained comparison is a feature: 0 < x < 1 means (0 < x) and (x < 1). Nice, but it changes short-circuit semantics.
Names resolve at call time, not definition time (closures see the current value of outer variables, a classic loop-closure bug).
Everything is an object: 1 and True compare equal (1 == True), and bool is a subclass of int. So [1, 2].count(True) counts True, not 1… except it counts both, because True == 1. Watch out in data cleaning.


Read & Refactor AI Code
The following AI-generated snippet looks reasonable but contains three bugs. Run it, observe the wrong behavior, find the bugs, and fix them in the editor.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Mutable default argument. The default list is created once, so the second call appends to the first call’s list. Fix: default to None and create the list inside.
is with floats. Identity comparison, not equality; 30.0 is not the same object as the literal in the function. Fix: ==, or better math.isclose for computed floats.
// instead of /. Floor division silently truncates the mean. Fix: /.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Explain precisely why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in terms of binary representation. Why is 0.5 stored exactly but 0.1 not?


Hint

Write 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 as sums of powers of 1/2. Which terminate?



Solution

IEEE-754 doubles store numbers as ±m × 2^e with a 53-bit significand. A decimal fraction is exactly representable only if it is a dyadic rational — a fraction whose denominator is a power of 2. 0.5 = 1/2 is dyadic: exact. 0.1 = 1/10 needs denominator 2 × 5; the factor 5 is impossible in binary, so 0.1 rounds to the nearest 53-bit binary fraction: 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.... Adding the two rounded values 0.1 + 0.2 gives a value whose rounded nearest double is 0.30000000000000004, one ulp above 0.3’s nearest double. Consequence for practice: never test float equality; test abs(a-b) < tol or math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=0.0). For exact decimal money/counting semantics use decimal.Decimal or integers.

Q2. What does this print, and why?








Hint

Closures capture variables, not values. When do the lambdas look up f?



Solution

[9, 9, 9]. Each lambda closes over the variable f; by the time they are called, the loop finished and f holds 3, so every call computes 3*3. Fix by binding at definition time: lambda f=f: f*f (default argument evaluated immediately), or use a factory function def make(f): return lambda: f*f. The same late-binding logic explains why a list of functions that reference a module-level config variable all change behavior when you reassign that variable.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (functions × strings × loops → bioinformatics). Write translate(seq) that translates a DNA string to an amino-acid one-letter string using the standard genetic code, handling (a) lowercase input, (b) a trailing partial codon, (c) stop codons marked *. Test on ATGGCCATTGTAATGGGCCGCTGAAAGGGTGCCCGATAG (you can hardcode just the codons you need, or a 64-entry dict). When you reach 0.2 NumPy, consider which parts of this problem could be vectorized — and which fundamentally cannot (hint: the lookup table is not arithmetic).
C2 (this page × 1.1 Descriptive statistics). Write a pure-Python function summary(xs) returning a dict with n, mean, median, min, max, computed without importing anything. Then check: what happens with an empty list, a list of one element, and a list containing None? Design your function’s error behavior deliberately (raise ValueError? skip None?) — this is exactly the design decision pandas makes for you with skipna=True.

title: 0.1 Python for Numerical Work
text:
7. Summary

Python names point to objects; types live on the objects, not the names.
/ is true division, // floors, % gives the remainder; floats are IEEE-754 binary — compare with math.isclose, never ==.
Comprehensions > loops for building collections; f-strings > string concatenation for output.
Functions returning None by default and mutable default arguments are top sources of silent bugs.
is checks identity; == checks equality; empty containers are falsy.
Closures look up variables at call time — late binding breaks loop-generated functions.
Pure-Python numeric loops are slow: the moment you have arrays of numbers, you want 0.2 NumPy, which pushes loops into compiled code and changes how you express numerical ideas entirely.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text: Inference answers the question every experiment asks: is this pattern real, or would chance produce it? Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty about a population quantity; hypothesis tests quantify how surprising the data would be under a “nothing is happening” model. Both are built on one idea — the sampling distribution of a statistic.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
1. Basic Concept
The standard error. A sample mean varies from sample to sample with SD ≈ \(s/\sqrt{n}\) — the standard error (SE). Small n means the SE is big means the sample mean is a shaky estimate of the population mean.
Confidence interval. A 95% CI for a mean is approximately
\[\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where the t-quantile widens the interval for small samples. Interpretation (get this exactly right): if the sampling procedure were repeated many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true mean — it is a property of the procedure, not a 95% probability statement about this particular interval.






Hypothesis test logic. State \(H_0\) (no effect) → compute a statistic measuring departure from \(H_0\) → the p-value is P(data at least this extreme | \(H_0\)). Small p = the null struggles to explain the data. It is not P(\(H_0\) | data).






Errors and power. Two ways to be wrong: Type I — declare an effect under a true null (rate = α); Type II — miss a real effect (rate = β); power = 1 − β, driven by effect size, n, α, and noise.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
2. Concept Questions

A 95% CI is (2.1, 3.9). Is “P(true mean is in (2.1, 3.9)) = 0.95” a correct reading?
Why does a p-value not tell you the probability the null hypothesis is true?
What does the t in “t-test” buy you over a z-test, and when does the distinction vanish?
Your test on n = 5 has p = 0.20. Which conclusions are valid: (a) “no effect exists”, (b) “effect not demonstrated”, (c) “need more data or a better design”?
Why is equal_var=False (Welch) the sensible default for two-sample t-tests?



Answers


No. The interval is now fixed — it either contains the mean or not. The 95% describes the procedure’s long-run success rate across hypothetical repetitions. (Frequentist probability attaches to procedures, not fixed quantities.)
The p-value is computed assuming the null is true; it can’t then assign that null a probability. It is P(data at least this extreme | H₀) — evidence about the data under H₀, not about H₀ given the data. That reversal is exactly Bayes’ rule, and frequentist testing deliberately doesn’t do it (a prior on hypotheses would be required).
t replaces the known population σ with the estimated s, adding uncertainty that widens critical values (t₀.₉₇₅,₄ = 2.78 vs z = 1.96). As df → ∞, t → z; by n ≈ 30–50 the difference is negligible.

and (c) only. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; a high p-value at tiny n is uninformative, not exculpatory. Never conclude “no effect” without a power/equivalence argument.

Real biological groups rarely have equal variances, and Student’s pooled t can inflate false positives under inequality; Welch’s correction keeps Type I error near nominal with negligible power loss — so it’s the robust default.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the two-sample experiment below, compute (a) Welch t-test, (b) the 95% CI of each group mean, (c) the 95% CI for the difference in means (bootstrap is fine). State the decision and the estimate-with-uncertainty sentence you would put in a report.


Solution







Report sentence: “Treatment increased the marker by an estimated 1.5 units (bootstrap 95% CI 0.3 to 2.7; Welch p = 0.02).” The CI is the quantitative claim; the p-value only grades the surprise under “no difference.” Also note the CI excludes 0 exactly when p < 0.05 (two-sided) — consistency check.

Exercise 2. Multiple testing preview, empirically: simulate 100 independent two-group experiments under the global null (α = 0.05 each). (a) Expected number of “significant” results? (b) Empirical probability that at least one is significant? (c) Repeat at α = 0.001. What family-wise lesson emerges?


Solution







At α = 0.05, ~5 false positives per 100-null family and ≈ 99.4% chance of at least one. The family-wise error explodes with the number of tests — the problem Bonferroni and FDR (12.3, 12.4) solve.

Exercise 3. Demonstrate the effect of skew on the t-test/CI: sample n = 10 from a lognormal; bootstrap the sampling distribution of the mean; compare the bootstrap CI to the t-formula CI. Which is trustworthy here, and what sample size restores the t-approximation (test empirically)?


Solution







At n = 10 the mean’s true sampling distribution is strongly right-skewed — the symmetric t-CI is a poor description (and its 95% coverage is off). The bootstrap CI inherits the skew. At n = 100 the CLT has done its work and the two CIs nearly agree. Lesson: t-methods assume approximate normality of the sampling distribution, which skewed small samples violate; alternatives are log-transform, nonparametric tests, or larger n.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

p-value misreadings (all wrong, all common): P(H₀ true) = p; p = 0.03 means “3% chance the result is chance”; p > 0.05 means “no effect”; p = 0.049 vs 0.051 is a meaningful difference. The p-value is one number about one conditional probability — treat it as such.
The t-test compares means; it does not “prove normality” — with n = 5 you cannot even check the assumption well. Prefer Welch + report effect size + CI.
Paired vs unpaired is a design property: repeated measures on the same unit demand paired analysis (ttest_rel); pairing halves the noise only if the pairing is real.
Effect size ≠ significance: at n = 100,000, a 0.1% difference gets p ≈ 0; at n = 5, a huge effect gets p ≈ 0.3. Report effect + CI, let n decide detectability, not importance.
One-sided tests halve the p-value but require pre-registered direction — switching sides after looking at data is p-hacking.
Stopping rules break calibration: “collect until p < 0.05” inflates Type I error far above 5% (the simulation drill adapts to demonstrate this).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Design mismatch: after is generated from before — paired structure. The unpaired test throws away the pairing and most of the power. Use ttest_rel (or test the differences).
Both printed conclusions are wrong: small p is not “96% chance the treatment works” (it’s P(data|H₀), not P(H₀|data) or power), and large p never “proves useless”. Correct sentence: “data would be surprising under no-effect (p = …)”.
Sequential peeking: continuing until significance guarantees eventual “significance” even under a true null — Type I error ≈ 100%. Fix: pre-set n, or use a formal sequential design (alpha-spending); simplest demonstration — fix n and rerun.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive why the SE of a mean is \(s/\sqrt{n}\) using the variance-addition rule from 1.3, and explain the practical arms race it implies: to halve the SE of the mean, how much more data do you need? To halve the noise of each measurement?


Hint

Write Var(x̄) = Var(Σxᵢ/n²) with independence, then take square roots twice.



Solution

With independent \(x_i\) of variance \(\sigma^2\): \(\text{Var}(\bar x) = \text{Var}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum x_i\big) = \tfrac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2 = \sigma^2/n\), so \(\text{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt n\) — square-root law. Halving the SE of the mean requires 4× the data; the SE of the mean is about precision of knowledge, and knowledge is expensive. Halving the noise of each measurement (σ) is an instrument/protocol question, not a statistics question — and it pays off in every subsequent analysis. First optimize measurement noise, then buy n.

Q2. Construct and demonstrate the “optional stopping” inflation: under a true null, run the peeking loop (test after every new pair, stop at p < 0.05 or n = 200). Estimate the realized Type I error. Compare to a fixed-n = 200 test. What does this say about A/B test dashboards that highlight “significance” daily?


Solution







Peeking inflates the false-positive rate from 5% to roughly 30–50% — the more checkpoints, the worse. Daily-looked-at dashboards with “significance” badges are exactly this experiment; the fixes are fixed horizons, sequential designs (alpha spending), or Bayesian monitoring with pre-agreed decision rules.

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (inference × 0.5 Data splitting). Two models score 0.81 and 0.84 accuracy on the same 250-sample test set. Use the binomial SE machinery to judge whether they differ; then design the evaluation protocol (repeated splits or K-fold, paired comparison per fold) that would let you test the difference honestly. What makes the paired fold-wise comparison better than comparing two independent error bars?
C2 (inference × 2.4 Accuracy of the full model preview). Fit a simple linear regression to 30 noisy points; use the standard errors of slope and intercept (available from scipy.stats.linregress or a small manual computation) to build 95% CIs. Now re-fit on 300 points of the same process. How do the SEs scale, and why does “collect 10× more data” not always shrink practical uncertainty (name the two components: sampling error vs measurement/bias)?

title: 1.4 Statistical Inference
text:
7. Summary

Inference = sampling distributions: SE = s/√n; means shrink noise by √n — 4× data per 2× precision.
CI: range of parameter values the data can’t refute (at the chosen level); it’s the procedure that has 95% coverage, not your interval.
p-value = P(data this extreme | H₀); never P(H₀), never “chance of being right.”
Welch two-sample t is the default; paired designs need paired tests; ranks for non-normal data.
Power depends on effect, n, α, noise — underpowered studies “fail” without evidence of absence.
Multiple tests and optional stopping break the 5% guarantee; corrections and fixed protocols restore it.
When assumptions are shaky, resample the data itself: bootstraps and permutation tests — 1.5 Resampling intuition.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text: When the formula for an uncertainty is messy or unknown — a median, a difference of AUCs, a ratio — resampling replaces the mathematics with computation: shuffle or resample the data you have, recompute the statistic many times, and look at the spread. It is the bridge between classical inference and the cross-validation you will use for every model.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
1. Basic Concept
The bootstrap treats your sample as a stand-in for the population: draw new samples with replacement, same size as the original, recompute the statistic, repeat. The variability across bootstrap replicates mimics the sampling variability of the statistic.






Let’s do that cleanly for the median — the statistic where formulas hurt:






The permutation test answers a different question — “is this association real?” — by shuffling labels to simulate a world where the null is exactly true, and asking how extreme the real statistic is among the shuffled ones:






The jackknife — leave one out, recompute, look at the spread — estimates bias and SE from n recomputations (cheap, deterministic, less flexible):

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why must bootstrap resampling be with replacement, and what would happen without it?
What null does a permutation test simulate, and why don’t we need to know any distribution’s shape?
When does the bootstrap fail even with lots of data? Give one statistic and one data structure.
How does a bootstrap CI for a mean compare to the t-formula CI for near-normal data — and for skewed data?
Conceptually, how is K-fold cross-validation (0.5) a resampling method, and what statistic does it resample for?



Answers


With replacement generates variability — each replicate is a new pseudo-sample whose composition differs (some points twice, some never). Without replacement every replicate is the original sample in a different order — zero variability, zero information.
The null of exchangeability: group labels carry no information, so any shuffling of labels is as probable as the observed one. The p-value counts how often shuffled data produces a statistic at least as extreme as observed — no distributional formula required, only the labels being exchangeable under H₀.

Extreme order statistics — the min/max (bootstrap resamples contain ≤ n distinct values; the max can never exceed the observed max, so its distribution is degenerate). (b) Dependent data — time series or spatial data: i.i.d. resampling destroys the dependence structure that the statistic is about (fixes exist: block bootstrap).

Near-normal: nearly identical (bootstrap ≈ t-interval, slightly wider with percentile method). Skewed: the bootstrap CI inherits the skew of the statistic’s sampling distribution — often more honest than the symmetric t-CI (1.4 Exercise 3).
CV repeatedly partitions the sample, recomputes model performance on held-out parts, and reads stability from the spread — resampling the rows rather than resampling within a statistic’s input. Bootstrap estimates the variability of a statistic; CV estimates the variability of an estimation procedure’s performance.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Bootstrap the difference in medians between two skewed groups (5000 replicates), report the 95% percentile CI, and compare with the CI you’d get from a difference-in-means t-interval. Which pair of estimates is the better summary for skewed data and why?


Solution







For skewed data the medians + bootstrap CI pair is the defensible summary: medians resist the tail, and the bootstrap CI carries the actual (asymmetric) uncertainty. The t-CI on means is dominated by a handful of large values and its symmetric shape misrepresents the uncertainty.

Exercise 2. Implement the permutation test for a difference in means as a reusable function perm_test(a, b, n_perm=10_000, seed=0), then apply it to (a) clearly separated groups, (b) identical distributions. Verify in case (b) that p-values are approximately uniform on (0,1) over 500 repeats — the defining calibration property of a valid test.


Solution







The uniformity check in (b) is the gold-standard self-test of any test implementation: under a true null, p-values must be ~Uniform(0,1), so P(p < α) = α. If your p-values pile up near 0 under the null, your permutation scheme is broken (usually: statistic computed on non-pooled data, or shuffling within groups).

Exercise 3. Bootstrap vs formula SE shootout. For n = 8, 30, 200 samples from a lognormal, compute (a) the t-formula SE of the mean, (b) the bootstrap SE of the mean, (c) the bootstrap SE of the median. Plot/inspect how the three quantities and their stability change with n. Write the two-sentence takeaway.


Solution







Takeaways: (1) formula and bootstrap SE of the mean agree closely — the bootstrap recovers textbook results, validating the machinery; (2) for skewed data the median’s bootstrap SE is smaller and its own sampling distribution is more stable — another argument for robust summaries on skewed biological measurements.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The bootstrap resamples observations, not noise: each replicate should reproduce the original sample size and structure (paired rows stay paired; per-group sizes preserved by stratified bootstrapping).
Percentile CIs under-cover for small n and skewed statistics — improvements (BCa) exist; know that “bootstrap CI” is a family, not one object. Report the method.
Permutation tests require exchangeability under H₀ — with confounded group assignments (e.g. all treated samples run on batch 2), shuffling labels tests the wrong null. Design before inference.
Number of replicates: 1,000–10,000 for CIs; more for tail quantiles. Monte Carlo error of a percentile ≈ \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}\) — at B = 1,000 the 2.5% quantile itself wobbles.
Bootstrap cannot see beyond the sample: it inherits your outliers and your range (the max degeneracy drill). If the sample missed the tails, the bootstrap is confidently wrong about them.
rng.choice vs rng.integers indexing: rng.choice(x, size=(B, n), replace=True) in one call is far faster than a Python loop of resamples — vectorize your resampling like everything else.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated bootstrap has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


replace=False — every “replicate” is just the original data minus one point (a jackknife in disguise); no bootstrap variability.
size=len(data)-1 — replicates must match the original n; smaller samples underestimate the statistic’s variance.
[5, 95] percentiles — that’s a 90% interval labeled as a CI; 95% needs the 2.5/97.5 percentiles. (Minor: a Python loop of 1,000 resamples is fine here but the vectorized form is idiomatic and 100× faster.)







Note the outlier: watch how the bootstrap CI for the mean is stretched rightward while stat=np.median would give a tight, stable interval — run both and compare.

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Explain precisely why the bootstrap estimate of a statistic’s SE converges to the true SE as n → ∞, and why the approximation is double (empirical distribution → population, plug-in resampling → true sampling distribution). Where does small n hurt first?


Hint

The bootstrap replaces F (unknown population CDF) with F̂ (empirical CDF). Two questions: how well does F̂ approximate F, and how well does the bootstrap world mimic the real one for your statistic?



Solution

The bootstrap is a plug-in: it pretends F̂ (the empirical distribution — the sample itself) is the truth, then simulates sampling from F̂. By the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem, F̂ → F uniformly as n grows, so for statistics that depend smoothly on the distribution (means, moments, regression coefficients), the bootstrap SE → true SE. The error is two-layered: (1) F̂ ≠ F (sampling error of the original study — unavoidable, shrinks as n grows), and (2) the statistic’s behavior in the bootstrap world ≠ its behavior in the real world (mild for smooth statistics, severe for extremes/discontinuous ones like the max). Small n hurts first through layer (2) for non-smooth statistics and through percentile-CI undercoverage — with n = 10, the empirical distribution has only 10 distinct values and every resample is a sparse remix of them.

Q2. Your permutation test compares a treated group (n = 6) to controls (n = 40). (a) How many distinct label assignments exist, and what is the smallest nonzero p-value the test can ever return? (b) What practical consequences does this have for small-n study design and for reporting “p < 0.001” from a permutation test with 6+40 samples?


Solution


\(\binom{46}{6} = 9{,}366{,}819\) distinct assignments (treated labels are indistinguishable among themselves). The smallest nonzero p is \(1/\binom{46}{6} \approx 1.07 \times 10^{-7}\) — so in principle tiny p-values are attainable. (b) The real constraint is resolution vs replicates: with B = 10,000 random permutations, the add-one p-value has resolution ≈ 10⁻⁴ and Monte Carlo error ~\(\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}\); reporting “p < 0.001” from 10⁴ permutations is not supportable — report “p < 10⁻⁴” or increase B. Design lesson: permutation tests inherit the exact-conditional guarantee but their resolution is bounded by combinatorics and B — small treated groups are fine for moderate p-values, hopeless for “highly significant” claims without huge B (or full enumeration).

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (resampling × 0.5 Data splitting). Implement a bootstrap comparison of two models’ test accuracies: fit both models on each of 200 bootstrap resamples of the training set, evaluate both on the same fixed test set, and build the CI of the accuracy difference. Then explain why this underestimates the uncertainty from training-set variation compared to refitting on fresh splits, and how the “.632 bootstrap” style corrections (4.5) address the overlap problem.
C2 (resampling × 4.6 Hyperparameter tuning preview). You tune a hyperparameter by picking the K-fold CV optimum, then report that optimum’s CV score as the performance estimate. Simulate this procedure under a null (no signal: y random) with 20 candidate values and show the optimistic bias (selected score vs true score on fresh data). Which resampling discipline (nested CV) fixes it, and what does this have in common with the optional-stopping bug of 1.4?

title: 1.5 Resampling Intuition
text:
7. Summary

Bootstrap: resample rows with replacement, same n, recompute — the spread across replicates estimates uncertainty for almost any statistic.
Permutation test: shuffle labels under exchangeability; the p-value is the rank of the observed statistic among shuffled ones; distribution-free by construction.
Jackknife: leave-one-out; cheap deterministic bias/SE estimates.
Percentile bootstrap CIs match t-CIs for tame data and outperform them for skewed statistics.
Failure modes: order statistics (max), dependent data, non-exchangeable labels, tiny n, and reading more precision out of B replicates than B provides.
Vectorize resampling: one rng.integers/choice call for all replicates.
Uncertainty about a statistic is solved; uncertainty about a model’s predictions is the subject of Part 4 — starting from why held-out data is the only honest judge: Part 2 builds the first models, and Part 4 formalizes their evaluation.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text: How do two variables move together? Covariance and correlation quantify co-movement; regression (Part 2) will model it. The skill here is knowing what r measures, what it ignores, and the four ways it lies.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
1. Basic Concept
Covariance averages the products of paired deviations:
\[\text{cov}(x, y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\]
Positive when variables move together, negative when opposed — but its magnitude depends on the units (expression levels in raw counts vs log-CPM give different covariances for the same relationship). The Pearson correlation fixes units by dividing both SDs:
\[r = \frac{\text{cov}(x,y)}{s_x s_y} \in [-1, 1]\]






Key reading: r measures linear association strength, not slope (slope lives in regression) and not agreement (r = 1 for y = x + 100, which disagrees by 100 everywhere).
Spearman correlation = Pearson correlation applied to ranks. It detects any monotone relationship and shrugs at outliers:






And the classical caution — curvature: quadratic data can have r ≈ 0 over a symmetric range even though the variables are perfectly dependent:

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is covariance useless for comparing relationships measured in different units, and what exactly does dividing by \(s_x s_y\) fix?
What is the relationship between r and the R² of simple linear regression?
Give two datasets where Spearman = 1 but Pearson < 1.
Does r = 0 mean “no relationship”? Does r = 0.9 mean “x causes y”?
One outlier flips your r from +0.6 to −0.6. Which coefficient is more trustworthy here, and why?



Answers


Covariance’s magnitude scales with the units of both variables (cov(x, y) = 5 for x in minutes is 300 for x in seconds). Pearson divides by the product of SDs — a pure number in [−1, 1] — so relationships are comparable across studies, units, and scalings.
For simple linear regression, \(R^2 = r^2\) — the fraction of y’s variance explained by the best straight line. r = 0.7 → the line explains 49%.
Any perfectly monotone but nonlinear pair: (x, eˣ), (x, x³) over positive x, (age, income) rising with diminishing returns. Ranks are identical; straightness is not.
No and no. r = 0 only rules out linear association (quadratics, U-shapes, interactions can be strong). r measures association; causation requires design (randomization, natural experiments) or much stronger modeling assumptions.
Spearman. A single point moved Pearson’s estimate violently because r is built from raw deviations — the outlier dominates both \(s_x\), \(s_y\) and the cross-products. Spearman caps any point’s influence at “one rank step.”

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — Anscombe’s quartet, cell 1. This classic dataset has 4 pairs with (nearly) identical mean, SD, r ≈ 0.816, and regression line — utterly different shapes. Build pair I and pair III, compute their summary statistics, and plot both.


Solution







Identical r, identical fitted line — because r and OLS are single-number summaries that different data structures can satisfy. Summary statistics compress away exactly the things you care about; plotting is not optional.

Exercise 2. Construct data where adding ONE observation flips the sign of Pearson r (from negative to positive), while Spearman barely moves. Report all three r values before/after.


Solution







The added point sits at the extreme corner, contributing huge cross-deviations \((x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\) — enough to outvote 40 points. Spearman only sees “new highest x, new highest y” — one rank step on each side. Any reported Pearson on real data should come with a scatterplot or a rank-correlation cross-check.

Exercise 3. For a bivariate normal sample (n = 30, true ρ = 0), empirically show the sampling distribution of r under the null, and verify that |r| > \(2/\sqrt{n-1}\) (rough 5% rule) happens about 5% of the time.


Solution







≈ 0.05: with n = 30, “noise correlations” of ±0.37 are routine. Two implications: small-n correlation claims need formal tests (1.4), and large correlation matrices (0.3 pandas drills) will always show impressive-looking r values somewhere — that’s multiplication of opportunities, not biology.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Correlation ≠ causation — and neither correlation nor its absence is about linear vs nonlinear: r ≈ 0 coexists with perfect functional dependence (the x² plot).
Range restriction and range enhancement: selecting only high-GPA applicants lowers r; mixing two clusters inflates it (Simpson’s paradox lives here — see Complex Questions).
Pearson needs rough linearity and tolerates outliers badly; Spearman needs only monotonicity but discards magnitude information (two datasets with identical ranks can have very different practical effect sizes).
Correlation matrices in high dimensions (10,000 genes → 50M pairs): extreme r values appear by chance alone (Exercise 3 logic × opportunities). Multiple-testing discipline (Part 12) applies to “top correlated pairs” lists.
Averaging correlations across groups is invalid (r is not on an additive scale — use Fisher z, or analyze per group).
Bootstrap or Fisher-z CI for r, never “r ± 0.05” from folklore. Formal test: stats.pearsonr returns the p-value alongside.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “correlation report” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


r ≠ slope and ≠ causation. The slope estimate is np.polyfit’s job, and “causes” needs design evidence, not correlation.
Averaging r across groups is invalid and hides sign flips; here group r’s may be +1 and −1, “averaging” to 0 while both groups have perfect (opposite) associations. Report per-group r (or Fisher-z average with justification).
r ≈ 0 ≠ no relationship. The U-shaped dependence is perfect; Pearson only tests the linear projection.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that for simple linear regression the fitted slope is \(b = r \cdot (s_y / s_x)\), and explain the two failure modes of “reading” r as if it were an effect size.


Hint

Write the OLS slope for standardized variables; then unstandardize.



Solution

Standardize both variables: \(\tilde x = (x-\bar x)/s_x\), \(\tilde y = (y-\bar y)/s_y\). For standardized data the OLS slope is \(\sum \tilde x_i \tilde y_i / \sum \tilde x_i^2 = (n-1)\,\text{cov}/(n-1)\,\text{var} = r\). Rescaling back multiplies by \(s_y/s_x\), giving \(b = r s_y/s_x\). Failure modes: (1) slope from r — r = 0.5 means nothing about units; a weak correlation with huge \(s_y/s_x\) can be a big effect. (2) r as slope — the same physical relationship yields different r if you restrict the x-range (range restriction lowers both spread and r) while the slope \(r s_y/s_x\) is more stable. Report both: r (strength of linear association), slope (effect per unit x), CI each.

Q2. The t-statistic for testing ρ = 0 is \(t = r\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-r^2)}\). Verify numerically that stats.pearsonr’s p-value matches the two-sided t-test with df = n−2, then explain what happens to that p-value’s meaning when you compute it for the largest of 10,000 gene-pair correlations.


Solution







The p-value is calibrated for one pre-specified pair. For the maximum over 10,000 pairs, the test is applied to the extreme order statistic of ~10,000 correlated tests: even under global null, the smallest p-value is routinely ≪ 0.05 (probability of at least one “significant” pair ≈ 1 − 0.95¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 1). The honest procedure re-tests the selected pair in fresh data or applies family-wise/FDR correction — the entire subject of Part 12.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (relationships × 0.3 pandas — Simpson’s paradox). Build 3 groups where within every group r(y, x) is positive, but pooled over all groups r is strongly negative. (Give group intercepts very different levels and equal within-group slopes.) Then answer: which correlation should a model use — and how does adding group dummies (2.6 Categorical predictors) resolve the conflict?
C2 (relationships × 9.2 PCA preview). Generate 3 correlated variables, compute the correlation matrix, and its eigenvalues. What does the dominant eigenvalue/eigenvector tell you about how many “real directions” the data has? Relate this to why the scatter-matrix drill of 0.4 becomes unreadable at 50 variables and PCA becomes necessary.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
7. Summary

Covariance is direction × scale; Pearson r standardizes it to [−1, 1]; Spearman replaces values with ranks.
r describes linear association only: U-shapes hide at r ≈ 0; monotone curves lose r < 1.
r² is explained-variance for a straight line; slope is r·(sy/sx) — never confuse strength with effect size.
One outlier can flip Pearson; Spearman caps that influence — report both when data is dirty.
Sampling noise gives |r| ≈ 0.3 routinely at n = 30; scanning many pairs manufactures “discoveries.”
Per-group correlation, plots, and range questions come before any causal sentence.
Association is a description; deciding whether a pattern would reappear in new samples requires probability and inference — 1.3 Probability essentials.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text: Descriptive statistics compress a sample into a few honest numbers: where is the center, how wide is the spread, what shape is the distribution. Every model diagnostic, every “significant difference,” every anomaly alert you will ever compute rests on these primitives — so the definitions (including the ones with silent variants, like population vs sample SD) must be reflexes.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
1. Basic Concept
Center. The mean \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i\) is the balance point; the median is the middle value by rank. They coincide for symmetric data; for right-skewed data, mean > median (a few large values drag the mean).
Spread. The variance is the average squared deviation from the mean. Two flavors:
\[s^2_{\text{pop}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \qquad s^2_{\text{sample}} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\]
The \(n-1\) (Bessel’s correction) in the sample version compensates for the fact that \(\bar{x}\) was estimated from the same data — deviations from an estimated center are systematically too small. Standard deviation is the square root, back in data units.






Position and shape. Quartiles split the sorted data into quarters; the IQR (Q3 − Q1) is the spread of the middle half — robust to outliers. Skewness measures asymmetry (positive = right tail).






Robustness ranking (how much a single extreme value can move the statistic):

mean, SD — sensitive (breakdown point 0%)
median, IQR — robust (breakdown point 50%)
trimmed mean — tunable middle ground

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the sample variance divide by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\)?
Your gene-expression distribution has mean 210 and median 85. What shape do you suspect, and which two numbers would you report?
Is the IQR affected by multiplying all values by 10? By adding one extreme value?
When is the mode the most informative measure of center?
What does ddof=0 vs ddof=1 change in np.std, and which does pandas use by default?



Answers


Deviations are taken from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data; the fitted center absorbs part of the variability, shrinking deviations. Dividing by the degrees of freedom \(n-1\) unbias the estimate of the population variance (for normal data, exactly).
Strong right skew (a minority of very high values). Report median and IQR (robust pair); if you must report the mean, report it with the median so the skew is visible.
Multiplying by 10: IQR scales by 10 (it’s in data units). One extreme value beyond the fences: IQR is unaffected as long as it doesn’t cross the 25th/75th percentiles — that’s the point of quartile-based spread.
For categorical or discrete data (“most common category”), and for multimodal continuous data where mean and median both describe nothing real (“typical patient: bimodal, modes at X and Y”).
ddof = delta degrees of freedom subtracted from n. ddof=0 → population formula; ddof=1 → sample formula. NumPy defaults to 0, pandas to 1 — mixing pandas and NumPy without noticing this is a classic silent bug.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write summarize(x) returning {"n", "mean", "sd", "median", "iqr", "min", "max"} using sample SD. Test it on normal data and on lognormal data; state which summary number changes most between the two and why.


Solution







The mean and SD blow up under lognormal data (they inherit the heavy tail), while median and IQR stay near their symmetric-data values — the empirical demonstration of robustness. Report median/IQR for skewed data.

Exercise 2. IQR outlier rule: flag values outside \([Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR},\ Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}]\) in the dataset below. Then compute z-scores and flag \(|z| > 3\). Compare the flagged sets and explain the disagreement.


Solution







The z-score rule uses the mean and SD — which the outlier itself inflates. One extreme value widened the SD so much that even the outlier isn’t 3 SDs out (masking). Quartile-based rules don’t have this self-blinding property: for small samples, prefer the IQR fence.

Exercise 3. Empirically verify Bessel’s correction: sample n = 5 points from a known distribution many times; for each sample compute variance with ddof=0 and ddof=1; average each. Which average converges to the true variance?


Solution







ddof=0 averages to \(0.8\sigma^2\) here (\((n-1)/n = 4/5\)) — a 20% underestimate, every time, silently. This is why the divisor choice is not a technicality.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

pandas vs NumPy ddof defaults disagree (pandas std/var use ddof=1; NumPy uses ddof=0). Numbers in mixed reports can differ by ~√(n/(n−1)) for no reason.
NaN handling differs: np.mean poisons, np.nanmean skips, pandas .mean() skips and warns differently — know which behavior produced a reported number.
Percentile interpolation: np.percentile linearly interpolates by default; small-n quartiles depend on this convention (9 conventions exist; R’s type=7 matches NumPy’s linear).
SD is not the “typical deviation” for skewed data: with a heavy right tail, most deviations are below the SD. IQR communicates spread more honestly there.
The mean minimizes squared error, the median absolute error — which is why least squares regression (Part 2) is mean-focused and least-absolutes-deviations is median-focused.
stats.mode behavior changed across SciPy versions (now returns a ModeResult object); pd.Series.mode is the stable, readable choice.
Descriptives ≠ inference: a summary is a claim about this sample; Part 1.4 is about claims regarding the population.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated summary function has three bugs. Run it on the test data and find them.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Population SD (ddof=0) — for a sample summary this underestimates spread; specify and use ddof=1.
No NaN policy — the function dies on the NaN (mean → nan, max → nan) without telling the caller whether NaNs were dropped. Make the policy explicit.
range on data containing NaN raises/propagates nan; also “range” is a fragile descriptives choice (a single typo’d value sets it) — min/max separately at most, or a robust span.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove (or verify by simulation) that the sample mean is the value \(c\) minimizing \(\sum_i (x_i - c)^2\), and the sample median minimizes \(\sum_i |x_i - c|\). What does each say about which errors the mean vs median take most seriously?


Hint

Differentiate \(\sum (x_i-c)^2\) in \(c\); for the absolute value, argue by moving \(c\) across data points and counting how many terms’ slope changes.



Solution

Mean: \(f(c)=\sum(x_i-c)^2\) has \(f'(c) = -2\sum(x_i-c)\), zero exactly at \(c=\bar{x}\) (second derivative \(2n>0\)). Median: \(g(c)=\sum|x_i-c|\) has slope \(= (\#\,\text{points} < c) - (\#\,\text{points} > c)\), which changes sign where the counts balance — the median. So the mean’s optimality is defined in squared error: a single far point contributes quadratically, dominating the objective — hence the mean chases outliers. The median’s objective is linear in each error: one far point costs the same as one near point — hence its robustness. This one paragraph explains robust statistics, why least-squares regression is outlier-sensitive, and why quantile regression exists.

Q2. Two labs each report SD ≈ 2.0 for the same assay. Lab A ran n = 5, Lab B ran n = 5,000. Construct a scenario where both reports are true, and explain which additional number distinguishes them (preview: it is not the SD).


Solution

Both labs can honestly report \(s \approx 2.0\) — SD describes individual measurement spread and barely depends on n. What distinguishes them is the precision of their estimated means: the standard error \(s/\sqrt{n}\) ≈ 0.89 for Lab A vs 0.028 for Lab B — a 30-fold difference. SD answers “how noisy is one measurement,” SE answers “how well do I know the center.” Confusing the two (reporting SD where SE is meant, or vice versa) is a notorious publication bug; the inference machinery that formalizes it arrives in 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (descriptives × 0.4 EDA). For the lognormal samples from Section 1, produce side-by-side: (a) histogram of x, (b) histogram of log x with a normal-density overlay scaled to the log data. Which single transformation converts all the robust-vs-sensitive summary disagreements (mean/median, SD/IQR) into non-issues, and what does that imply about when those disagreements matter?
C2 (descriptives × 3.1.5 AUPRC preview). A screening cohort has 1% disease prevalence. Compute the mean/median of the binary label vector and explain, in descriptive-statistics language, why accuracy is a nearly useless summary for a classifier on this data (predicting all-healthy scores 99%). Which descriptive statistic of the confusion matrix would you report instead, and why is it robust to the prevalence imbalance?

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
7. Summary

Center: mean (balance, sensitive) vs median (rank, robust); skew shows as mean − median.
Spread: SD for symmetric data, IQR for skewed; ddof=0 vs 1 is a real bias, and pandas/NumPy disagree by default.
Quartiles + IQR fences detect outliers without being blinded by them; z-scores can be.
NaN policy is part of the statistic: nan-skipping is a decision, not a default to trust blindly.
Mean ↔︎ squared error, median ↔︎ absolute error: robustness follows from the loss function.
SD describes single measurements; SE describes the precision of a mean — next pages formalize this.
Summaries describe samples; to argue about populations you need probability and inference: 1.2 Relationships first asks how two variables move together.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text: Probability is the language in which every model speaks: a predicted probability, a p-value, a 95% interval, a likelihood. This page drills the rules, the three distributions that do most of the work in ML (binomial, Poisson, normal), and the one formula — Bayes’ rule — that most people’s intuition gets wrong.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
1. Basic Concept
The rules. For events A and B:

Complement: \(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\) — “at least one” questions become “1 minus none.”
Addition: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\) — the intersection is counted twice, subtract once.
Multiplication / conditioning: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)\); independence means \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), so for independent events conditioning changes nothing.
Bayes: \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\) — the flip between “evidence given cause” and “cause given evidence.”







Random variables and their machines. A distribution assigns probability to outcomes. The three workhorses:









Distribution
Models
Parameters
scipy




Binomial
# successes in n independent yes/no trials
n, p
stats.binom


Poisson
# events in fixed time/space (counts, reads)
λ (rate)
stats.poisson


Normal

μ, σ
stats.norm









Expectation and variance are the distribution’s center and spread: \(E[X] = \sum x\,p(x)\); for the sum of independent variables, means add and variances add (this additive rule powers everything from portfolio risk to the SE of a mean).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
2. Concept Questions

A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific; prevalence is 1/1000. Roughly what fraction of positive results are true positives, and which two quantities fought each other in the Bayes computation?
When does Poisson model counts well, and what does it assume that binomial does not?
What is P(X = 4.0) for a continuous random variable, and what do we evaluate instead?
Why do variances add but standard deviations don’t?
If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.8, what is P(A ∪ B)?



Answers


About 9%. The fight: the evidence actually observed (true positives, \(0.99 \times 0.001\)) versus the much larger pool of false positives generated by the huge healthy majority (\(0.01 \times 0.999\)). Base rate dominates when prevalence is low.
Poisson fits counts of events in a fixed window when events are rare and independent (reads overlapping a gene, mutations per kb). It assumes events occur with a constant rate and no upper bound; binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials n.
Zero — a point has no width, so its probability mass is 0. We evaluate \(P(X \le x)\) (CDF) or \(P(a < X < b)\) (density integrated over the interval).
Variance adds because the cross-terms of independent variables average to zero: \(\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X)+\text{Var}(Y)\). SD is the square root of that sum, and square roots don’t add: \(\sqrt{a+b} \ne \sqrt a + \sqrt b\).
\(P(A\cup B) = 0.5 + 0.8 - 0.5\times0.8 = 0.9\).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the full Bayes computation. Disease prevalence 0.1%, test sensitivity 99%, specificity 99%. Compute (a) P(disease | positive), (b) the same for prevalence 10%, (c) how high specificity must be at 0.1% prevalence for PPV ≥ 50%. State each result as one sentence.


Solution








9% — a positive result is usually false at 0.1% prevalence. (b) 92% — the same test is excellent in a high-risk population. (c) specificity ≈ 99.90% — the false-positive rate per healthy person must be driven below the true prevalence. Same machine, three different decisions — this is why screening policies depend on prevalence, not just on test quality.


Exercise 2 — Monte Carlo verification. Verify analytically-computed probabilities by simulation: (a) at least one six in 4 rolls; (b) P(Binomial(20, 0.3) ≥ 10); (c) P(Normal(0,1) within ±1.5). Report simulated vs exact to 3 decimals.


Solution







Note the pattern — sf(9, ...) for “≥ 10” (sf is P(X > k), so use k−1). Monte Carlo with N = 10⁶ carries ~0.05% MC error; agreement to 3 decimals is expected, and this verify-by-simulation habit will debug countless probability computations later.

Exercise 3 — the law of total probability in a lab setting. 1% of samples are contaminated. Contaminated samples fail QC 80% of the time; clean samples fail 2% of the time. What fraction of samples fail QC? Given a sample failed QC, what’s the probability it was contaminated?


Solution







Two-step structure: total probability pools the failure rate across the two sample types; Bayes re-weights to ask about the cause. Even a 40× higher failure rate for contaminated samples only gets you to 27% — because clean samples are 99× more numerous. Always ask what population produced this positive.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

P(A|B) vs P(B|A) — transposing the conditional is the prosecutor’s fallacy; DNA-match statistics are its most famous victim. Every Bayes computation should start by naming which conditional you have and which you want.
Independence is not “small correlation” and not “no obvious relationship” — it is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) exactly. Rarely true for biological measurements (batch, relatedness, shared environment).
pdf values are not probabilities — stats.norm.pdf(0) ≈ 0.4 yet P(X=0) = 0; the density integrates to probability. Only CDFs and intervals carry probability meaning.
sf(k) = P(X > k) (strictly greater) — the classic off-by-one: P(X ≥ 10) = sf(9), not sf(10). Write the inequality before writing the function call.
Poisson has variance = mean; real count data routinely violates this (overdispersion) — the reason negative-binomial models exist in RNA-seq DE analysis (12.6).
CLT applies to standardized sums of many independent contributions — not to heavy-tailed data at small n, and not to highly skewed counts at n = 5.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screening calculator” has three bugs. Run it, then fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Complement misuse: the stray “× 3” multiplies the none-detect probability by 3, producing a negative “probability”. The complement of “at least one” is “none”, full stop: \(1 - 0.9^3\).
sf off-by-one: sf(8) = P(X > 8) = P(X ≥ 9); for P(X ≥ 8) use sf(7).
pdf differences are not probabilities — subtracting densities is meaningless. Integrate: cdf(1.96) - cdf(-1.96).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the 9% PPV result symbolically and explain in terms of the Bayes numerator and denominator why increasing sensitivity barely helps at low prevalence, while increasing specificity helps enormously.


Hint

Write PPV \(= \frac{sp\,\pi}{sp\,\pi + (1-sc)(1-\pi)}\) and ask: which term shrinks when sens ↑ vs spec ↑, at \(\pi = 0.001\)?



Solution

PPV \(= \dfrac{\text{sens}\cdot\pi}{\text{sens}\cdot\pi + (1-\text{spec})(1-\pi)}\). At \(\pi = 0.001\): the numerator term is ≈ sens × 0.001 — small no matter how good sens is (bounded by prevalence itself). The denominator’s second term is \((1-\text{spec}) \times 0.999\) — nearly the whole healthy population times the false-positive rate. Raising sens 0.99 → 0.999 multiplies the numerator by ~1.009; raising spec 0.99 → 0.999 divides the false-positive term by 10. At low prevalence, PPV is governed by specificity — which is why screening programs chase specificity and why confirmatory (more specific) tests follow any positive screen.

Q2. Two independent watchtowers detect fires with probabilities 0.8 and 0.7 respectively. Given exactly one detection occurred, what is the probability it was tower 1? Compute symbolically and verify by Monte Carlo.


Hint

Enumerate the four detection outcomes with their probabilities; condition on the two “exactly one” outcomes.



Solution

Outcomes: both \(= 0.8 \times 0.7 = 0.56\); neither \(= 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.06\); only-1 \(= 0.8 \times 0.3 = 0.24\); only-2 \(= 0.2 \times 0.7 = 0.14\). Given “exactly one”, it was tower 1 with probability \(0.24/(0.24 + 0.14) = 0.632\).






Note the method: enumerate + condition, or simulate — both beat formula-hunting when the event structure gets any more complicated.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (probability × 0.5 Data splitting). A test set has n = 50 samples with true accuracy p = 0.8. Compute the exact probability (binomial) that the measured accuracy is ≥ 0.9 (i.e., ≥ 45 correct). Now compute the same for n = 500. What does each number say about the credibility of “90% accuracy!” claims at the two sample sizes — and connect this to the binomial SE formula used in 0.5 Q2.
C2 (probability × 12.4 FDR preview). You test 10,000 genes for differential expression at α = 0.05; none are truly differential. (a) How many false positives do you expect? (b) What’s the probability of at least one? (c) If 100 are truly differential with 80% power, what is the positive predictive value of your “significant” list? This single calculation is the entire motivation for FDR correction — predict what q-values do before learning them.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
7. Summary

Complement turns “at least one” into “1 − none”; addition subtracts the double-counted intersection.
Conditional probability is the primary object; independence is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), not an adjective.
Bayes’ rule converts P(evidence|cause) to P(cause|evidence); at low prevalence, specificity dominates PPV.
Binomial = n trials; Poisson = counts in a window (variance = mean); Normal = the CLT’s destination.
pdf values are densities, not probabilities; CDF/sf carry probability, and sf is P(X > k) — mind the off-by-one.
Variances add for independent sums; SDs don’t.
Verify any analytic probability with a Monte Carlo one-liner — cheap, and it catches unit/interval bugs.
With probability as the language, the next step is the sentence structure of statistics: estimation and testing — 1.4 Statistical inference.
